title: Wien's Displacement Law
short_intro: Wien's displacement law states that the wavelength corresponding to the maximum spectral emissive power of a blackbody is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature. It forms a fundamental bridge between thermodynamics and electromagnetic radiation.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct numerical calculations involving Wien's constant, peak wavelength shifts due to temperature changes, and qualitative understanding of blackbody radiation curves.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of Wien's displacement law from Planck's radiation law, application to stellar classification, colour-temperature relationships, and frequency-form formulations.

prerequisites: Degrees of freedom and blackbody absorption

concept_notes.heading: Physical Origin of Wien's Law
bullets: A blackbody emits a continuous spectrum of radiation whose distribution depends entirely on its absolute temperature.
As temperature increases, the total energy emitted per unit area increases, and the peak of the emission spectrum shifts towards shorter wavelengths.
The relationship is encapsulated by the inverse proportionality between peak wavelength and absolute temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Wien's Constant (b)
bullets: The proportionality constant b is known as Wien's displacement constant.
Its experimentally determined standard SI value is approximately 2.898 x 10<sup>-3</sup> m·K.
It is invariant for universal blackbody radiation across all materials exhibiting ideal blackbody behavior.

concept_notes.heading: Frequency Form of Wien's Law
bullets: Wien's law can also be expressed in terms of frequency where the peak frequency ν<sub>max</sub> is directly proportional to absolute temperature T.
The frequency form is given by ν<sub>max</sub> = alpha T, where alpha is a different constant derived from Planck's distribution.
Note that ν<sub>max</sub> / T does not correspond directly to c / lambda<sub>max</sub> due to the asymmetry of the blackbody distribution curve when plotted against wavelength versus frequency.

concept_notes.heading: Astrophysical Applications
bullets: Used extensively in astrophysics to determine the surface temperatures of stars by observing their peak emission wavelengths.
Hotter stars (like Sirius) appear blue due to peak emission in the ultraviolet or short-wavelength visible spectrum.
Cooler stars (like Betelgeuse) appear red due to peak emission shifting toward longer infrared wavelengths.

derivations.title: Derivation of Wien's Displacement Law from Planck's Law
derivations.conditions: Start from Planck's spectral radiance law for a blackbody: E_\lambda(\lambda, T) = \frac{2\pi h c^2}{\lambda^5 (e^{\frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}} - 1)}
steps: Differentiate the spectral emissive power E_\lambda with respect to wavelength λ and set the derivative equal to zero to find the maximum: \frac{dE_\lambda}{d\lambda} = 0.
Let x = \frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}. Taking the derivative yields an equation of the form (5 - x)e^x = 5.
Solve the transcendental equation numerically to find the root x ≈ 4.965114.
Substitute back x = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{max} k_B T} = 4.965, which gives \lambda_{max} T = \frac{hc}{4.965 k_B} = b.

formula_sheet.name: Wien's Displacement Law (Wavelength Form)
formula_sheet.variables: \lambda_{max} = \text{ wavelength of maximum emission}, T = \text{ absolute temperature}, b = \text{ Wien's constant}
formula_sheet.units: \lambda_{max} \text{ in m}, T \text{ in K}, b \text{ in m\cdot K}

formula_sheet.name: Wien's Constant Value
formula_sheet.variables: h = \text{ Planck's constant}, c = \text{ speed of light}, k_B = \text{ Boltzmann's constant}

formula_sheet.name: Wien's Law (Frequency Form)
formula_sheet.variables: \nu_{max} = \text{ frequency of maximum emission}, T = \text{ absolute temperature}

formula_sheet.variables: E_{\lambda, max} = \text{ peak spectral radiance}, C_1 = \text{ constant}
formula_sheet.conditions: Derived by substituting \lambda_{max} into Planck's law

formula_sheet.variables: \lambda_{max1}, \lambda_{max2} = \text{ peak wavelengths at temperatures } T_1, T_2

formula_sheet.name: Energy Density Maximum
formula_sheet.variables: u_{\lambda, max} = \text{ maximum spectral energy density}

formula_sheet.name: Star Color Index Relation
formula_sheet.conditions: Assuming stellar atmosphere acts as a blackbody emitter

formula_sheet.name: Wien's Approximation (Short Wavelength Limit)
formula_sheet.equation_html: E_\lambda(\lambda, T) \approx \frac{2\pi h c^2}{\lambda^5} e^{-\frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}}
formula_sheet.conditions: High frequency or low temperature limit of Planck's law

graphs_and_experiments.title: Blackbody Radiation Spectral Distribution Curves
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Multiple curves of Spectral Emissive Power (E_\lambda) vs. Wavelength (λ) at different increasing absolute temperatures (T_3 > T_2 > T_1). Show that each curve has a distinct peak that shifts to shorter wavelengths as temperature increases, and the area under the curve increases.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates both Stefan-Boltzmann law (total area under curve increasing with T<sup>4</sup>) and Wien's displacement law (λ<sub>max</sub> moving left towards the origin as T rises).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in TGT/PGT for identifying correct qualitative graphs and matching peak shifts with temperature changes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Logarithmic Plot of Wien's Displacement Law
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of \ln(\lambda_{max}) versus \ln(T) with a negative slope equal to -1 and a y-intercept equal to \ln(b).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms the inverse power-law relation \lambda_{max} \propto T^{-1} in linear logarithmic form.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT level conceptual questions regarding data linearization.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stellar Spectra Comparison Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Intensity versus wavelength profiles for a red star, a yellow star (Sun), and a blue star plotted on the same axes.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visually proves that hotter stars emit peak radiation at shorter wavelengths (blue end) compared to cooler stars (red end).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Applied in numerical problems determining stellar surface temperatures from spectral observations.

solved_numericals.question: The sun radiates maximum energy at wavelength 4700 Å. Assuming the sun acts as a blackbody, calculate its surface temperature. (Given Wien's constant b = 2.89 x 10<sup>-3</sup> m·K)
solution_steps: Identify given values: \lambda_{max} = 4700 \text{ Å} = 4700 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}, b = 2.89 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m\cdot K}.

solved_numericals.question: If the temperature of a blackbody is increased from 300 K to 900 K, by what factor does the peak wavelength change, and what is the shift in the peak wavelength if its initial value was 9660 nm?
solution_steps: Substitute temperatures: \frac{\lambda_{max2}}{\lambda_{max1}} = \frac{300}{900} = \frac{1}{3}. The peak wavelength decreases by a factor of 3.
Calculate new peak wavelength: \lambda_{max2} = \frac{9660 \text{ nm}}{3} = 3220 \text{ nm}.
solved_numericals.answer: Wavelength decreases by a factor of 3; shift is 6440 nm towards shorter wavelengths.

solved_numericals.question: The peak of the emission spectrum of a certain star is found at \lambda_{max} = 580 nm. Find the maximum frequency of emission \nu_{max} using the frequency form of Wien's law, given h = 6.63 x 10<sup>-34</sup> J·s, k<sub>B</sub> = 1.38 x 10<sup>-23</sup> J/K, and b = 2.898 x 10<sup>-3</sup> m·K.
solution_steps: First find the temperature of the star using wavelength form: T = \frac{b}{\lambda_{max}} = \frac{2.898 \times 10^{-3}}{580 \times 10^{-9}} = 4996.55 \text{ K}.
Use the frequency form constant relation: \nu_{max} = \left(\frac{2.821 k_B}{h}\right) T.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: The radiating body is an ideal blackbody capable of absorbing and emitting all frequencies uniformly without reflection losses. Limitation: Real bodies (grey bodies) have emissivity less than 1 and vary with wavelength, causing deviations from the ideal Wien's law shift.

Assumption: Quantum statistics (Planck's law) governs the derivation. Limitation: Classical Rayleigh-Jeans law fails at high frequencies (ultraviolet catastrophe), which Wien's displacement law correctly avoids by matching the exact peak.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The peak frequency ν<sub>max</sub> is equal to c / lambda<sub>max</sub>.
common_misconceptions.why: Because the functional form of the blackbody spectrum is asymmetric when plotted against wavelength versus frequency, the maxima occur at different corresponding spectral points.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Wien's law gives the wavelength where total emitted energy is maximum.
common_misconceptions.correct: Wien's law gives the wavelength where spectral emissive power per unit wavelength interval (E_lambda) is maximum.
common_misconceptions.why: Total energy integrated across all wavelengths follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law (E = σT<sup>4</sup>), not a single wavelength.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Wien's displacement constant b is a fundamental constant like c or h.
common_misconceptions.correct: b is a derived constant resulting from a combination of fundamental constants (h, c, k<sub>B</sub>) and a transcendental number.
common_misconceptions.why: It is not an independent fundamental constant of nature.

quick_revision: Wien's law states \lambda_{max} T = \text{constant} (\approx 2.898 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m\cdot K}).
Higher temperature means shorter peak wavelength (bluer color).
Peak spectral radiance scales as E_{\lambda, max} \propto T^5.
